title: Minimum Operations to Make Median of Array Equal to K
statement:
You have an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`. One operation adds 1 to, or subtracts 1 from, a single element of your choice. Return the smallest number of operations after which the median of `nums` is exactly `k`.

Here the median of an array of length n is the value at index `floor(n / 2)` (0-indexed) once the array is sorted in non-decreasing order. So for an even length it is the larger of the two middle values.
notes:
## Intuition

Sort the array. In the final array the element at index `middle = floor(n / 2)` must be `k`, everything before it must be at most `k`, and everything after it at least `k`. So the sorted middle element has to move to `k`, every earlier element above `k` has to come down to `k`, and every later element below `k` has to come up to `k`. Each of those moves is the cheapest possible for that element, and nothing else needs to change, so this greedy total is optimal. Because the array is sorted, the elements that need fixing sit right next to `middle`, and each scan can stop at the first element that is already fine. (A brute force could try sending every element below, to, or above `k` in all 3^n ways.)

## Approach

1. Sort `nums` in increasing order and find `middle = floor(n / 2)`.
2. Start `operations` at `|nums[middle] - k|`, the cost of moving the median itself.
3. Walk left from `middle - 1` while `nums[i] > k`, adding `nums[i] - k` for each.
4. Walk right from `middle + 1` while `nums[i] < k`, adding `k - nums[i]` for each.
5. Return `operations`.

## Example 1, step by step

Sorted `nums` is `[2, 5, 5, 6, 8]`, `k = 4`, `middle = 2`.

- `nums[2] = 5`, so `operations = 1`.
- Left: `nums[1] = 5 > 4` adds 1, giving `2`; `nums[0] = 2` is not above 4, so stop.
- Right: `nums[3] = 6` is not below 4, so stop at once.

The answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n): the sort dominates; the two scans are O(n) together.
- Space: O(1) besides the sort.

## Pitfalls

- For an even length the median is the upper middle, index `n / 2`, not `n / 2 - 1` (Example 3).
- Moving only the median is not enough: in `[5, 5, 5]` with `k = 1`, after changing one 5 to 1 the median is still 5; two elements must reach 1, costing 8.
- The total can reach about 2·10^14, so use a 64-bit integer (`long`) in Java and C.
- Sort with a numeric comparator in JavaScript; the default sort compares numbers as strings.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `middle` | index of the median in the sorted array |
| `operations` | total operations counted so far |
| `i` | index being checked while scanning outward from `middle` |

narration.2: Sort numerically so the median sits at a fixed index.
narration.3: The median is at index floor(n / 2), the upper middle for an even length.
narration.4: The median element itself must move all the way to k.
narration.6: Scan left from the median while elements are still above k; sorting means the rest are fine.
narration.7: Each such element must come down to k so it does not exceed the median.
narration.9: Scan right from the median while elements are still below k.
narration.10: Each such element must come up to k so it is not smaller than the median.
narration.12: Every forced move was counted once at its minimum cost.
